10              Plaintiff,              ORDER                             

11   v.                                                                   

12   Nationwide Insurance Company of America,                             
    et al.,                                                              
13                                                                        
               Defendants.                                               
14                                                                        
15        Pending  before  the  Court  are  three  motions  filed  by  pro  se  Plaintiff  Gregory 
16   Sullivan:  a motion to remand (Doc. 9), a motion to allow electronic filing (Doc. 21), and 
17   a motion to rule on previously filed motions (Doc. 23).              
18        Plaintiff filed the motion to remand on July 22, 2019, and Defendant Nationwide 
19   Insurance Company of America (“Nationwide”) filed a response on August 2, 2019.  (Doc. 
20   15.)  Under LRCiv 7.2(d), Plaintiff had the option of filing a reply by August 9, 2019.  
21   Plaintiff failed to do so,1 and the motion became ripe on the following business day, August 
22   12, 2019.  Ten days after the motion to remand became ripe, Plaintiff filed a motion to 
23   allow electronic filing and a motion to rule on the pending motions.  (Doc. 23.) 
24        The Court has many cases pending before it and many motions on which to rule.  
25   Careful consideration and resolution of pending motions requires review of the briefs, 
26   research of the legal issues, contemplation, and precise drafting.  All of this takes time.  
27                                                                        
    1    Perhaps the “Response to the Declaration of Mark E. Hartman of Opposition for 
28   Remand Motion to Remand and Vacate Mandatory Initial Discorvery [sic] Pilot Project” 
    (Doc. 17) was intended to be the reply, but it was not titled or docketed as such. 
1   The Court has inherent power to control its docket.  Thompson v. Hous. Auth. of City of 
2   Los Angeles, 782 F.2d 829, 831 (9th Cir. 1986).  The Court is mindful of the need “to 
3   secure the just, speedy, and inexpensive determination of every action and proceeding,” 
4   Fed. R. Civ. P. 1, and strives to handle all matters with both wisdom and expediency.  
5   Although the Court understands that waiting for rulings is frustrating, litigants are expected 
6   to exercise reasonable patience before filing motions for rulings.  Ten days is too soon. 
7        Nevertheless, the Court will address the motion to remand now because it can be 
8   easily and quickly resolved.                                         
9        Diversity jurisdiction exists when there is complete diversity of citizenship between 
10   the plaintiff and the defendants and the amount in controversy exceeds $75,000, exclusive 
11   of interests and costs.  28 U.S.C. § 1332.  A controversy meets this requirement when “all 
12   the persons on one side of it are citizens of different states from all the persons on the other 
13   side.”  Strawbridge v. Curtiss, 7 U.S. 267 (1806).  A corporation, whether incorporated in 
14   a state of the United States or in a foreign country, is “deemed a citizen of its place of 
15   incorporation and the location of its principal place of business.”  Nike, Inc. v. Comercial 
16   Iberica de Exclusivas Deportivas, S.A., 20 F.3d 987, 990 (9th Cir. 1994).   
17        The Notice of Removal states that “Defendant Nationwide is a Wisconsin company 
18   with its principal place of business in Ohio” (Doc. 1 ¶ 2), and indeed, the Complaint alleges 
19   that Nationwide’s “principal place of business is [in] Ohio” (Doc. 1-3 ¶ 2).  The motion to 
20   remand does not assert otherwise.   The Notice of Removal states that Plaintiff is a 
21   “resident” of Arizona (Doc. 1 ¶ 2), which is insufficient to establish citizenship for diversity 
22   purposes, Kanter v. Warner–Lambert Co., 265 F.3d 853, 858-59 (9th Cir. 2001), but the 
23   Complaint affirmatively alleges that Plaintiff is a “citizen” of Arizona (Doc. 1-3 ¶ 1).  Thus, 
24   the  parties  are  diverse.    And  the  motion  to  remand  confirms  that  “Plaintiff  seeks 
25   compensatory damages of $250,000,” so the amount-in-controversy requirement is met.  
26   The motion to remand will be denied.                                 
27        Next, the Court will deny the motion to allow pro se electronic filing.  Electronic 
28   filing requires parties to code their filing so that they are properly docketed electronically.  
       Docketing requires legal training which Plaintiff does not possess.  When electronically 
2||    filed documents are not properly docketed, they are not easily retrievable by the Court on 
  ||  its case management reports. 
4          Plaintiff seems to believe there are two other pending “motions” awaiting rulings, 
5 ||  but one appears to be the August 1, 2019 motion for reconsideration (Doc. 13), which the 
6 ||  Court denied on August 2, 2019 (Doc.  14), and the other appears to be the “Response to 
7\|    the Declaration of Mark E. Hartman of Opposition for Remand Motion to Remand and 
8 ||  Vacate Mandatory Initial Discorvery [sic] Pilot Project” (Doc. 17), which is not a motion. 
9          Accordingly, 
10          IT IS ORDERED that the motion to remand (Doc. 9) is denied, the motion to allow 
11 ||  electronic filing (Doc. 21) is denied, and the motion to rule on previously filed motions 
12||    (Doc. 23) is granted in part and denied in part. 
13          Dated this 23rd day of August, 2019. 
14

14                                                                        
    Nationwide  Insurance  Company  of                                   
15   America                                                              

16                  Counter Claimant,                                     

17   v.                                                                   

18   Gregory R. Sullivan                                                  

19                  Counter Defendant.                                    

20                                                                        

21        Pending before the Court is Plaintiff/Counter Defendant Gregory R Sullivan’s 
22   motion seeking reconsideration of the Clerk’s Office’s July 24, 2019 minute order taking 
23   no  action  on  Sullivan’s  application  for  entry  of  default  due  to  Defendant/Counter 
24   Claimant Nationwide Insurance Company of America (“Nationwide”) having already 
25   filed an answer (Doc. 13.)                                           
26        Sullivan asserts Nationwide’s answer was untimely pursuant to Rule 12 of the 
27   Federal Rules of Civil Procedure.  (Doc. 13 at 1.)  In fact, Nationwide’s answer was 
28   timely pursuant to Rule 81(c)(2), which governs civil actions after removal from state 
       court:   “[a]  defendant who did not answer before removal must answer or present other 
2||    defenses  or  objections  under  these  rules  within  the longest of  .  .  .  (A)  21  days  after 
       receiving ... a copy of the initial pleading .. . , (B) 21 days after being served with the 
       summons for [the initial pleading], or (C) 7 days after the filing of the notice of removal 
5||    is filed.”  Nationwide filed its  answer (Doc.  6)  on July  17,  2019,  exactly 7  days  after 
6||    filing  the  notice  of removal  (Doc.  1.)   Thus,  the  answer  was  timely  filed.   See  e.g., 
7\|    Cariaga v. Bank of Am., 2011 WL 13233680, *2 (D. Haw. 2011). 
8          Moreover, pursuant to Rule 55(a), a party is subject to default only when the party 
      has “failed to plead or otherwise defend.”  As such, a default will not be entered after a 
10 ||  party files an answer—even a  late-filed answer.  See e.g.,  Gardner v.  Health Net,  Inc., 
      2011 WL 13269707, *2 (C.D. Cal. 2011).  Thus, even if Nationwide’s answer had been 
  ||  untimely (which it was not), default could not be entered because the answer was filed 
13}|    before Sullivan sought default. 
14          Accordingly, 
15          IT IS ORDERED that Sullivan’s motion for reconsideration (Doc. 13) is denied. 
16          Dated this Ist day of August, 2019. 
17
